subject: Mathematics
title: Golden Ratio and the Fibonacci Sequence
summary: Count a sunflower's seed spirals and you often get 34 and 55. They come from the Fibonacci sequence, whose ratios settle on the golden ratio, 1.618…

notes.title: Golden Ratio and the Fibonacci Sequence

keyPoints: **Fibonacci sequence:** 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, …: each term is the sum of the two before it.
Ratios of consecutive terms (8/5 = 1.6, 13/8 = 1.625, 21/13 = 1.615 …) approach the **golden ratio φ = (1 + √5)/2 ≈ 1.618**.
Squares with Fibonacci sides tile a near-golden rectangle; quarter arcs through them draw the **golden spiral**.
Sunflower seeds grow about **137.5°** (the golden angle) apart, so they pack without gaps; seed spirals often come in consecutive Fibonacci counts such as 34 and 55.

list: Many flowers: 3, 5 or 8 petals (lily 3, buttercup 5, cosmos 8)
Not every spiral is golden: the nautilus shell's spiral, for example, is not.
Each new seed or leaf grows about 137.5° round from the last (360°/φ²).
This angle never lines seeds up in straight rows, so they fill the head without gaps.
A simple fraction of a turn, like 135° (3/8), lines seeds into spokes with gaps.

simulation.reason: The claim that 137.5° packs best is only convincing when students can try to beat it: moving the angle by a fraction of a degree breaks the pattern, simple fractions collapse into spokes, and the spiral counts come out of the seeds. Choosing their own starting numbers tests whether the ratio really needs Fibonacci's 1, 1.
simulation.objective: Change the turn between seeds and find the angle that packs best, then test whether any start leads to φ.
instructions: Move the angle slider and watch the seeds; try 135°, 137°, 137.5° and 138°.
Compare the closest two seeds and the biggest hole for each angle.
At 137.5°, colour the spirals with 21, 34 and 55.
Enter your own two starting numbers and watch the ratio.
